13 year old Mary Phagan, a child laborer at the National Pencil Company, where Frank was director, was strangled to death on April 26, 1913 and found dead in the factory's cellar the next morning. The prosecution relied heavily on the testimony of Jim Conley, a janitor at the factory, who many historians consider the real culprit of the murder.

In August a guilty verdict was announced and then a lynch mob arrived at the prison in 8 cars. An electrician cut the telephone wires, members of the group emptied the gas from the prison's automobiles, handcuffed the warden, seized Frank, and drove away. The 175-mile (282 km) trip took about seven hours at a top speed of 18 miles per hour (29 km/h) through small towns on back roads. Lookouts in the towns telephoned ahead to the next town as soon as they saw the line of open cars pass by. A site in Phagen's hometown had been prepared, complete with a rope and table supplied by former Sheriff William Frey.

The crowd included souvenir hunters who cut away parts of Frank's shirt sleeves. One onlooker rallied to have the body cut into pieces and burned, and began to run around, screaming, whipping up the mob. Judge Newt Morris tried to restore order, and asked for a vote on whether the body should be returned to the parents. When the body was cut down, Frank's face and chest was stomped upon; Morris quickly placed the body in a basket, and it was driven out of town. In Atlanta, thousands besieged the undertaker's parlor, demanding to see the body; after they began throwing bricks, they were allowed to file past the corpse.
